content: Inhaled budesonide is a commonly used corticosteroid for managing asthma. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of budesonide compared to a placebo in treating chronic asthma in both children and adults. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search, including the Cochrane Airways Group Trial Register, reference lists of relevant articles, and abstracts from major respiratory society meetings between 1997 and 1999. They also contacted study authors to identify additional trials. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials comparing budesonide to placebo in children and adults with chronic asthma. A total of 43 studies, involving 2801 participants, met the inclusion criteria. In individuals with asthma not treated with oral steroids, budesonide significantly improved several measures of lung function. Specifically, it increased forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) by a Weighted Mean Difference (WMD) of 3.7% predicted (95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.1 to 7.2%). Morning peak expiratory flow (PEF) improved by 29 L/min (95% CI: 22 to 36 L/min), and evening PEF improved by 21 L/min (95% CI: 13 to 29 L/min). Although variations in symptom reporting across studies limited the ability to pool data, all high-quality studies consistently showed significant improvements in asthma symptoms with budesonide compared to placebo. However, health status outcomes were not reported in the included studies. The risk of withdrawal from trials due to asthma exacerbations was significantly lower in participants treated with budesonide compared to placebo, with a relative risk of 0.17 (95% CI: 0.09 to 0.33). Doses of 500–800 mcg/day appeared to produce slightly greater improvements than lower doses, but no additional benefit was observed with higher doses. One high-quality randomized controlled trial demonstrated that budesonide significantly reduced the daily requirement for oral prednisolone and increased the number of patients who were able to discontinue prednisolone entirely, compared to placebo. There was no significant difference in the risk of side effects such as oropharyngeal soreness, hoarseness, or oral candidiasis between budesonide and placebo. However, the long-term risk of adrenal insufficiency was not reported in the included studies. The authors concluded that this review strongly supports the use of budesonide for the treatment of chronic asthma. Current consensus guidelines recommend adjusting the dose of inhaled corticosteroids based on individual patient needs. The evidence from this review does not support routine dose escalation beyond 800 mcg/day.
